prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, reaching fractional uncertainties of 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for B012, Katori and Ye. The physics is one simple mechanism that is fully understood. At the magic wavelength the lattice light shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil shifts, and every remaining systematic (lattice light shifts, collisions, blackbody radiation) has been tracked down and modelled. The result has been reproduced by independent laboratories at roughly 1e-18, and the clocks resolve gravitational redshift across millimetres. The credited names fit the two halves of the achievement: Katori proposed the scheme and made the early strontium demonstrations, and Ye's group took accuracy, stability and many-atom control to the frontier. The round-1 exchange answered the main questions I had, and none of the new arguments changed my judgement. The chair's summary shows six members on B012. I note that count but do not use it as evidence. What decides it for me is that this is the only candidate where I can state the mechanism, the independent confirmation and the full credit in a few sentences, which I cannot do for B057 or B036.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains lineage and kind. The 2005 prize covered the comb and the 2012 prize covered ion control, and a lattice clock is a measurement capability rather than a discovery about nature. The fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark matter, a redefinition of the second) are still prospective. Credit is also not airtight: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Boyd and the ion-clock groups lie outside the pair, and I have not been able to check the 2001 to 2005 priority record against documents. A fair critic could say that a prize for a precision tool, awarded before its science return, is early. I think the established results (redshift over millimetres, agreement of independent clocks at 1e-18) answer this, but they do not remove it.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 but asks whether the committee should also credit the ion-clock lineage or the ultrastable-laser work, and says the 1e-18 and redshift results belong to Ye's group and need checking against the early record.
responses.response: I think the ion-clock and stabilised-laser contributions are real but belong to a different architecture and a different citation. Adding names would break the three-person limit and blur the lattice-specific claim, which is the only claim I think is distinct from 2005 and 2012. I agree with you that the 2001 to 2005 priority record must be read before the final ballot, and that the citation should say what is Katori's (the concept and the first demonstrations) and what is Ye's (accuracy, stability and many-body control). My draft citation names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 level, so that both appear. I do not regard your lineage through Hall's laboratory as a reason for you to abstain, because you disclose it and no joint work exists, but the committee should record it.

responses.point: Olsson asks for the citation to be written narrowly around the lattice-clock concept and its realization, and for exact priority among Katori, Takamoto, Lemonde and the JILA group to be checked.
responses.response: We agree, and in round 2 I propose the wording explicitly. 'Optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms' names the architecture and does not read as general frequency metrology. It leaves ion clocks, which use a different trapping principle, outside the claim and does not exclude them. On priority, I accept that Takamoto and Lemonde cannot be waved away. Still, the proposal of magic-wavelength trapping and the first strontium demonstration both trace to Katori, and the accuracy frontier traces to Ye, so the pair covers concept and realization. The fact that a prize leaves out junior co-authors and a parallel French effort is a structural property of any three-person limit, not a defect of this choice. I also remain at ease with your University of Tokyo fellowship disclosure, because you propose no one from your own institution.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved to B012 and now treats IceCube (B029) as a candidate for a later year because of the Baikal and AMANDA credit problem and the unresolved astrophysical interpretation.
responses.response: I share your reading, and it matches the argument I made against my own B057 in round 1: an unsettled credit list is a reason to wait, and the same logic applies to IceCube. I would add a point to your answer on timing. The redefinition of the second is a decision of a standards body, and the Nobel criterion should rest on the demonstrated science alone. If the committee waited for it, a metrological timetable would set a prize date, and I do not want that. I would still be glad to see the chair record in the minutes that the diffuse-flux discovery in B029 is robust, so that its deferral reflects attribution and not doubt about the result.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B036 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene) as lead, arguing that the central observations are reproduced and stable even though the pairing mechanism is not, and asks what would make it ready.
responses.response: You made the best case on the list for B036 and moved me on one point: the prize need not rest on the pairing mechanism, since the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated insulators at the magic angle are the credited discovery. Three things still keep it below B012 for me. I cannot yet say whether the superconductivity is intrinsic to the flat band or sample dependent. The credit tangle (Bistritzer versus MacDonald on theory; Cao, Fatemi, Dean and Young on the experimental side) has not been checked in the record. And the field is moving quickly enough that a better-defined citation may exist in two or three years. I would be comfortable with B036 in a later year, and I keep it as a serious alternative. I do not think waiting costs the discovery anything, and I do think B012 is ready now.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B029 (IceCube), argues that the diffuse flux is a robust discovery by nature rather than a model, and notes that every member proposing names for B029 chose the same trio.
responses.response: I accept the distinction you draw: the diffuse flux is a measurement of nature and not a tool, which I take seriously, since I concede the same objection against B012. But the agreement on the three names was reached from the proposals, whereas Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson say they cannot defend that trio on the evidence of who made the decisive contributions, and the chair has moved away from it. Agreement among nominators says little about the structure of credit inside a collaboration of hundreds with Baikal and AMANDA predecessors. You told us that you would not block B012. I take that as an honest position and hope the committee records that the diffuse-flux case rests on the science and is held back by the naming problem. I do not read the thin opening support as a scientific argument against B029.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record from 2001 to 2005 for magic-wavelength trapping and the first strontium lattice clocks (Katori, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Ye) supports exactly two names; I rely on recollection and not on the documents.
How much the 2005 and 2012 prizes reduce the novelty of lattice clocks for the full committee, and whether the narrow citation wording is enough to answer that.
Whether B057 could be given a fairer attribution set including the HgTe prediction within the three-person limit; if so it might be scientifically deeper than the clock.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene will be settled soon enough for B036 to overtake the clock in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B012: I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye and no tie to the other credited names. My Gothenburg environment is close to the Chalmers community of Johansson and Olsson, but I know of no joint work with any credited candidate. I have noted the disclosures by Kroll (lineage through John Hall's laboratory) and Olsson (University of Tokyo fellowship), and neither changes my view of the science. I have no tie to the B057 or B036 candidates.
